files.text:
On weather and still water

The Pond
in the Rain

A mirror, a squall, and the mirror again: what the wind and each drop do to the water, why the water goes grey, and what the sun finds after.

Still water under a bank of trees is the most exact mirror most of us will ever see out of doors. Stand at the edge and look across, and the willows on the far side hang upside down beneath themselves, every trunk carried on below the waterline, the sky laid in pale between the branches. You are looking at a glancing angle, and at a glancing angle water is a far better mirror than it seems from above. Straight down it gives back about two parts in a hundred and you see the mud; toward the far bank more than half of the light that reaches your eye has come off the surface. Then the first drop lands.

Wind first

A summer shower announces itself on water before it arrives. The light goes first: the bright gaps of sky between the trees turn to slate, and the mirror, which can only give back what it is shown, goes dull with them. Then, far off across the lake, a grey wall with its foot on the water: the rain itself, seen side on, leaning a little with the wind that drives it, swallowing the far trees one after another. Just ahead of it comes the gust. You can watch it cross the pond as dark patches racing over the surface, the ones sailors call cat’s paws. Each is a patch of ripples a few millimetres high, too small to see one by one, but enough to break the mirror where they pass, so that the water there shows its own dark instead of the sky. The willows lift and toss all at once, the long switches at the top of the crowns most of all.

The first drops

The first drops of a shower are usually the largest. Big drops fall faster than small ones, close to nine metres a second against two for drizzle, so they outrun the rest of the cloud’s rain and arrive on their own, a few to a pond, each one a sound you can place. A drop four millimetres across punches a crater several times its own size, throws a thin crown up round the rim, and then the crater fills from below so fast that the water overshoots and leaps up the middle as a column. Arthur Worthington drew this by the light of an electric spark in the 1870s and photographed it in the 1890s; his book of the pictures, A Study of Splashes, came out in 1908, and the column still carries his name. Often its tip pinches off as a single droplet, which rises a little further, falls back, and makes a second, smaller ring inside the first.

A train of rings

What spreads from the crater is never one ring but a train of them. On water the shortest ripples, held taut by surface tension, travel faster than the longer waves behind them, so the finest crests run out ahead and the train lengthens as it goes, smoothing as it spreads. They widen by twenty or thirty centimetres a second, and within a second or two viscosity has taken them out altogether. Rings from different drops pass straight through one another and come out unchanged on the other side, which is why a pond in light rain looks like a net of circles rather than a muddle.

Seen across the water they are not circles at all but flat ellipses, and you see them less as bumps than as bends in the reflection. Each crest tilts a strip of the mirror toward you or away, so a ring shows as a curved band where the picture of the trees is pushed up into the sky and pulled down into the trunks. Near the far bank, where the angle is lowest, a tilt of a degree or two is enough to swap the reflection of a leaf for the reflection of a cloud.

A pond in rain is not wetter. It is only rougher, and roughness is grey.

Why the pond goes grey

In a steady shower hundreds of drops land on every square metre every second, and the rings never get the chance to be seen one at a time. The surface becomes a fine, restless roughness, every few millimetres tilted a different way, and each point of it now reflects not one place on the bank but a scatter of them: a little sky, a little trunk, a little dark water under the leaves. The eye averages that into grey. The sharp edges go first, then the shapes, then the difference between the bright gaps and the dark trees. Under the rain cloud the sky is darker too, and a rough surface gives back the average of it rather than its brightest parts, so the pond darkens as it greys. The rain falling between you and the far bank veils the willows a little, and against their leaves, if you look, you can just make out the streaks.

The sound of it

You can hear the size of the rain. Drizzle on a pond is almost silent. Drops of about a millimetre make the hiss we think of as the sound of rain, and the hiss is not the impact at all: as the little crater closes it pinches off a tiny bubble at its floor, and the bubble, shuddering into its round shape, rings at around fourteen thousand cycles a second for a few thousandths of a second. Hundreds of them together are the hiss. Bigger drops trap bubbles only now and then, larger and lower, which is the plink and plop of a heavy shower, and the largest of all, the drops that collect on leaves and fall from the ends of branches, land with a single deep plunk you can hear from the other side of the water.

After

When the shower moves on, the trees go on raining for a while. Water that has run along the leaves gathers at their tips and at the low points of the branches and falls from the same places again and again, a fat drop every second or two at first, then every five, then every ten as the leaves drain. They make the biggest rings of all, close in under the bank, and between them the surface quiets. The fine roughness is the first thing to go, a few seconds after the last drop, and the reflection comes back out of the grey all at once: the trunks, the bright gaps of sky, the line of the far shore. Then the colour, which seems to have been rinsed. The willows are greener than they were before, and the water is holding them still again. If the sun comes through behind the last of the cloud, its reflection is not one image but a path of glints, each a small wave tilted just so to send the sun into your eye: narrow and close-packed far out, breaking into separate sparks as it comes toward you.

Fin

# rain-pond A summer squall crossing Corot's willows, scrolled through as one weather event, with the painting taking part. The painting is cut at its far waterline: above it the bank is Corot's, below it the pond is made live, a mirror of that bank seen at a glancing angle. Scroll, and: 1. **Calm.** A still mirror, in Corot's own slightly silvery colour. 2. **The squall comes in.** The light goes (the bright sky darkens first, contrast drops, the colour cools to a blue-green grey with the willows still olive) and a slanted grey wall of rain, with a ragged leading edge and darker streaks hanging from the cloud, advances across the far bank from the left, swallowing the willows. Its reflection comes with it. 3. **Wind and the first drops.** A gust: dark cat's paws race across the water (patches of fine ripples that kill the mirror where they pass) and the painted willows move, crowns swaying as masses, the light switches fluttering, the trunks still. The first fat drops land, with crowns and Worthington jets. 4. **Downpour.** Sheets of rain sweep across in waves, leaning with the wind; the far bank is half lost in haze; the surface is covered in small rings with splash points and little jets standing up, and near you drops bounce up as crowns; the reflection breaks into a grey shimmer. 5. **Clearing.** The rain eases from the left as the squall moves off to the right: half the pond calm, half still grey. Last drips fall from the willows. 6. **Sun.** A warm light passes across the bank, a glitter path opens on the water under the bright cloud, and the colour comes back fuller than it was at the start. A finger or pointer drawn over the water leaves a wake; a tap lets a single drop fall. ```html
``` The section is the scroll runway (`480svh`); the stage inside it is pinned while you scroll through, and the whole shower happens inside that runway. The `` must be a picture of a bank **cut at its waterline** (the bottom edge of the image is the line where bank meets water). The piece is a full-bleed band: the stage's whole width and about 88% of its height, bank above and water below. The painting covers the bank's area anchored at the waterline, so on a wide screen its sky runs off above the band (it is kept in the texture, for steep ripples to reflect) and on a phone it is cropped around `data-focus`. Only the top (~8.5%, a long, quiet, slightly uneven contour where the sky meets the paper) and the bottom (~5%) fade; every other pixel is the painting and its reflection, sharp. Or call `rainPond(section, options)` yourself; it returns `destroy()`. The section also gets `section.rainPond` with `destroy()`, `drop(x, y, mm)` (fractions of the water, size in mm) and read-only `progress` / `state`. ## Options | attribute | option | default | | |---|---|---|---| | `data-seed` | `seed` | `11` | the shower is the same on every visit for one seed | | `data-density` | `density` | `1` | scales the number of drops (and how grey the pond goes) | | `data-strength` | `strength` | `1` | scales every drop and wake | | `data-focus` | `focus` | `0.36` | 0-1 across the painting: the centre of the crop on narrow screens | | `data-water` | `water` | by aspect | water height / bank height (0.56 landscape, 0.95 portrait) | | `data-mono` | `mono` | `0.85` | the painting's colour at the start (1 = Corot's full colour); the storm cools and drains it to ~0.58, the sun brings it to 1.18 | The options object wins over the attributes. `--rpd-runway` (CSS) sets the runway length. ## Events All bubble from the section, for sound to be wired to later. | event | detail | when | |---|---|---| | `rain-pond:drop` | `{ size, x, y, kind }` | a drop lands. `size` in mm (0.4-4.5 for rain, 3.4 for a tap); `x`, `y` 0-1 across / down the water (0 = the far bank); `kind` is `rain`, `tap` or `droplet` (the secondary droplet a Worthington jet throws back). In the shower this fires 150-250 times a second: a sound layer should treat small sizes as a hiss, not one sample each | | `rain-pond:drip` | `{ size, x, y }` | a fat drop (5-6.5 mm) from a branch tip lands near the bank | | `rain-pond:rain` | `{ intensity }` | the shower's strength (0-1) changes by more than 0.05 | | `rain-pond:gust` | `{ strength }` | the gust arrives (once each time it is scrolled into) | | `rain-pond:sun` | `{ warmth }` | the sun breaks through (once each time) | ## Theming | variable | default | | |---|---|---| | `--paper` / `--rpd-paper` | `#f3f0e8` | what the picture melts into at its edges | | `--rpd-body` | the painting's lower third, darkened | the pond's own colour, seen where it does not reflect | | `--rpd-sky` | the painting's top rows | what the steepest ripples reflect | | `--rpd-mist` | a grey of the painting's mean | the veil of rain and the colour a rained-on pond goes | | `--accent` | clay | keyboard focus ring | ## The real thing What was modelled (notes in the brief, from Worthington's *A Study of Splashes*, Pumphrey & Crum, Oguz & Prosperetti and Le Méhauté's work on gravity-capillary rings): - **Glancing view.** The far bank is 2.4 times further than the bottom of the frame; each row of the water grid is a strip of pond whose world width grows as 1/distance and depth as 1/distance². A ring is a flat ellipse (about 1:1.6 near you, about 1:4 under the bank) and crawls slower on screen the further away it is. - **Reflection.** A mirror of the bank across the waterline. The surface slope toward or away from you tips the reflected ray up or down the bank by twice the slope (so a 2% slope moves the picture ~40 px, and a steep crest shows the open sky above the trees); a sideways slope shifts it by less (times the sine of the glancing angle), which is why reflections smear vertically. Fresnel (Schlick) with the facet's own tilt: the far water is a bright mirror, the near water shows more of its own dark body. - **Rings.** The wave equation plus surface tension (short ripples outrun long ones, so a drop leaves a train of 3-5 crests, finest outside) and viscosity (short ripples die first); rings superpose and pass through each other; they fade within 1.5-2.5 s. - **Drops.** A crater with a lip; drops over 1.2 mm rebound (the column springing back); over 2.3 mm a crown flashes for 60 ms and a Worthington jet rises and falls in 0.2 s, its reflection below it, and over 2.8 mm the jet usually pinches off a droplet that rises, falls back at ~0.35 s and makes its own small ring. A bright fleck marks each splash for ~0.1 s. - **The shower.** Size sorting: the first drops are few and fat (mostly 2.4-4.5 mm, simulated, with crowns and jets), the steady shower is many and small (0.4-1.6 mm: 300-450 a second on a desktop, two to three hundred rings alive at once, each a short train of crests with a bright splash point, gone in about half a second), the easing mixes both. - **Small rings** are written straight into the slope field rather than simulated: a two-or-three-crest packet leaving the splash at ~25 cm/s, flattened by the same perspective, fading with a 0.28 s time constant. The grid (2 x 1.5 css px) is too coarse to carry millimetre drops' ripples without turning them into grid noise. - **Grey.** Recent rain (a lagged measure, ~1 s up, ~1.5 s down) roughens the whole surface below the sim's scale: a fine field of slopes re-dealt ten times a second in place (no drift: there is no wind) that scatters each reflected ray by a few tens of px, so the trunks and gaps of sky still read as broken vertical patches; a little of a softened bank, a little sky, a grey veil and a slight darkening. The far shoreline loses its crisp edge. Rain streaks: thin, slightly slanted, of varied length, drawn so they only ever lighten what is behind them: visible against the trunks and dark water, lost against the sky, never over the paper. - **Drips.** Nine fixed branch tips on the painting; each drips on its own beat, quick while the leaves run with water (every ~2 s), slower as they drain (every ~7 s), then not at all. The drop is seen falling, lands a little in front of the bank, and makes the biggest rings of all. - **Squall and gust.** A rain shaft seen from afar is a grey, leaning curtain from the cloud base to the water, streaked by denser and thinner shafts; it brings a gust ahead of it. Cat's paws are patches of capillary ripples raised by the gust: they move with the wind (here ~260 css px/s near you, slower in perspective far off), and because they are rough they show the water's dark instead of the mirror. - **Glitter path.** The sun's reflection on a rippled surface is a column of glints, each a facet tilted to send the sun to your eye: narrow and dense far out, wider and sparser toward you. Simplified: the squall is drawn, not simulated (no real depth; the veil sits on the bank's plane); the willows' sway is a displacement of the painting, not a tree model, so the sky behind them drifts a little with it; the small rings are drawn a little larger and longer-lived than a millimetre drop's (crests 4-8 px apart near you, so the slope texture can carry them); the far pond's sub-pixel rain rings are represented by the roughness field; the bank is one plane at one distance, so reflections of trees nearer or further than the bank are mirrored at the same line; no bubbles (only their sound would show), no wind. ## The weather `weather(p)` in `rain-pond.js` gives, for scroll progress `p`, every quantity the shader and the rain need: storm darkness, the squall veil's leading and trailing edges (it moves left to right), haze, wind, gust, rain sheets, where on the pond it is raining (another pair of edges), the sun's warmth and the passing band of light, and the glitter. All of it is applied in one function, `atmos()`, to a point of the bank, and the water reflects the bank through the same function, so the veil, the storm light and the sun appear in the reflection by themselves. The willows' movement is a displacement of the bank texture (`sway()`), by height above the water: nothing at the trunks, mass sway and flutter in the crowns. Phases at a glance (p): calm 0-0.06, squall 0.06-0.27, wind and first drops 0.27-0.4, downpour 0.4-0.62, clearing 0.62-0.8, sun 0.8-1. ## How it works - **Grid.** About 720 x 190 cells on a desktop (2 css px across, 1.5 down), stepped 72 times a second on the CPU, with viscosity and a hyperviscosity that takes out grid-scale ripples. Each row has its own Laplacian weights (1/width², 1/depth² of that strip of pond), which is all the perspective the physics needs. The sides and near edge absorb (the pond goes on); the far bank reflects. - **Texture.** World slopes across and toward you, square-root encoded (fine steps near flat, still room for a crater) into an RGBA8 texture, plus the splash flecks. No float textures. - **Shader.** One fragment shader draws the bank (1 texel per device px), the water (mirror sample displaced by the slope, blurred bank mixed in by roughness, Fresnel, body colour), the colour (desaturated until the rain clears) and the top and bottom fades (a mask built once per size). - **Air.** A 2D canvas over it draws the streaks, crowns, jets, droplets and falling drips, masked by the same soft edge. - **Schedule.** Intensity, the share of fat drops, drip beats and colour are functions of scroll progress; the drops themselves come from a seeded Poisson process in real time. Stop scrolling in the shower and it keeps raining; left alone for 40 s, the shower passes on its own and comes back when you scroll. ## Tuning Constants at the top of `rain-pond.js`: `RATIO` (how far the bank is), `GLANCE` (how flat the rings are), `SPEED` / `TENSION` / `VISCOSITY` / `HZ` (ring speed and how much of a train each drop makes), `DECAY` (how long rings last), `SLOPE` (encoding range), `PEAK` (drops a second in the shower), `dropR` / `dropA` (simulated ring size and strength by drop size), `SMALL`, `RING_V`, `RING_T` (the analytic small rings), `DRIPS` (branch tips as fractions of the painting; move them if you use another picture). The shower's shape is `rateAt`, `fatAt`, `dripPeriod` and `satAt`. Another painting works if it has a clear far waterline near its bottom edge and some sky above the trees (the sky is what rings flash with). Crop it at the waterline. ## Accessibility and reduced motion - The painting is decorative (`alt=""`, `aria-hidden`), the canvases are `aria-hidden`. - The figure is focusable: Enter or Space lets a drop fall, the left and right arrows draw a wake across. A visually hidden `aria-live` line names the phases as you scroll through them (the first drops, steady rain, the rain eases, drips from the willows, the mirror returns). - `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce`: no runway and no rain. The scene just after the shower, in full colour, with four rings caught part way out. Nothing moves and touch does nothing. - `touch-action: pan-y` on the figure: a vertical swipe always scrolls the page (a finger moving over the water as it scrolls leaves a wake); taps drop. - Print shows the plain painting. ## Cost - Nothing runs while the pond is still: at the start, after the weather has come to rest, off screen and in a hidden tab. Scrolling while the water is still only redraws when the colour changes. - In the downpour, the heaviest moment: about 5.7 ms of script a frame on a laptop (measured: `section.rainPond.state.ms`, a running average), with small rings capped at 220 at once; one full-screen draw (about twenty texture reads a pixel on the water), a few hundred strokes on the air canvas. 60 fps. - While the weather is moving (wind, the veil's drifting shafts, sheets, the glitter path) the loop runs; left alone for 40 s it all comes to rest (rain passes, wind drops, glitter fades) and the loop stops, until the next scroll. - Canvas DPR capped at 2. The painting is 3775 px wide (1.2 MB webp): sharp at DPR 2 on a 1440-1920 px desktop and in the phone crop. - Without WebGL or with a cross-origin image, the painting stays, its sky fading into the paper. ## Credits - Camille Corot, *A Pond in Picardy*, ca. 1867. The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Open Access (CC0). See `assets/credits.json`. - The height-field water is ripple-pool's (this repo), laid out in perspective.
